records.why: Keeping code next to its tests and away from cluster YAML stops product engineers from editing production objects by hand. CI can build an image from this repo without needing cluster credentials. Reviewers who know the service own this merge.
notes: Source of the commit that becomes newsfeed-service:v1827.
Service config that is not a Kubernetes object stays with the code.
CI configuration is referenced, not forked, so gates stay consistent.
A green build produces an image. A later write lands in the manifests repo.

records.name: Infrastructure Terraform
records.what: Infrastructure definitions as code: VPC, cluster, node groups, load balancers, databases, IAM, DNS, queues, and observability agents. This is desired infra state, not desired workload state. App developers never run Terraform to ship a feature. Platform engineers change this repo when the substrate itself must change.
records.why: Cloud click-ops cannot be reviewed, reverted, or tested. Encoding the account in Terraform makes plane B visible and rare. The daily feature path should never need a plan/apply. If it does, the platform is missing an abstraction.
notes: Invoked (plan/apply), then exits. Opposite personality from Argo CD.
Remote state is locked. Concurrent apply is a failure, not a race you hope to win.
A new node group or database is this repo. A new replica of news-feed is not.
The cluster this poster deploys onto was created from this repository.

records.name: Deploy manifests
records.what: This repository is the desired Kubernetes state: Deployments, Services, HPA, Ingress, and related YAML. After a green image publish, CI writes the image digest into a Deployment here. Argo CD is the only process that applies that intent to the cluster. Humans review the GitOps pull request. They do not apply it.
records.why: Separating manifests from application source is what makes GitOps honest. The cluster has one writer for workload intent. CI never talks to the Kubernetes API. If the digest is not in this repo, Argo CD has nothing new to sync.
notes: This is desired workload state, not application source and not infrastructure.
Promotion is a Git write, not a pipeline step that calls kubectl.
Reviewers here think about replicas, probes, resources, and rollouts.
Argo CD watches this repo continuously.

records.name: Results back to the PR
records.what: Suite completion posts status checks and comments on the pull request. Required statuses block merge. Artifacts are retained for debug. The PR is the inbox. Chat is not the system of record.
records.why: If results live in Slack, merge policy cannot see them and history cannot explain them. Putting the result on the PR is what makes fail-closed real. Reviewers and branch protection read the same object.
notes: Status plus logs plus debug artifacts.
A red suite is a blocked merge, not a conversation starter.
Artifacts have a retention policy. They are not eternal.
The same comment shape is used for every suite.

records.name: Scheduler
records.what: Binds pods to nodes. Once Argo CD has been accepted, the scheduler places the new replica set. It does not pull images. kubelet does that after the bind, using the node's cloud identity.
records.why: Placement is policy: resources, topology, taints, affinity. Without a scheduler you have a pile of machines. With one, a digest becomes a running process on a node that can actually pull it.
notes: Triggered by unbound pods in the API.
Writes bindings. Does not pull images.
Respects topology spread and disruption budgets.
Unschedulable pods are a signal for the cluster autoscaler.

records.name: Search
records.what: Index of posts and people. Fed asynchronously from the queue, not from the request path that renders a feed. Query path comes from news feed or a dedicated search API.
records.why: Search is a derived view. Building it on the write path of a post is how you miss SLOs. Feeding it from Kafka keeps the system of record thin and lets you rebuild the index.
notes: Triggered by indexers consuming Kafka.
Stores search documents.
Not the source of posts.
Managed service, provisioned by Terraform.

records.name: Cloud SQL
records.what: System of record for users, posts, and the relational slice of the feed. Provisioned by Terraform, consumed by services, never migrated by a CI deploy job. Backups and replicas are plane-B concerns.
records.why: Relational data does not belong in a container filesystem. A managed database is the boring store that survives a node drain. Schema changes are versioned and applied by a deliberate job, not by the rolling deploy of v1827.
notes: Triggered by application services.
Created by Terraform, not by Argo CD.
The services that own the tables talk to it.
A feature ship does not apply a database.

records.name: 1. Commit and open the PR
records.what: A developer writes newsfeed-service on the platform toolchain and commits. Local checks already match CI. They push and open a pull request. This is the only human trigger that will follow.
records.why: If shipping requires a second human ritual after the PR, the path will be bypassed. Starting the whole poster with a commit is the operating rule: people write Git, machines do the rest.

records.name: 10. Observe and feed back
records.what: Each pod and node emits metrics, logs, and traces through OpenTelemetry. SLIs drive HPA, canaries, and pages. A bad deploy is rolled back through Git, not by re-running a deploy script.
records.why: The path is a loop. Telemetry is how the next change gets smarter and how this change gets reverted if it was wrong.

records.name: 2. CI gates
records.what: The pull request triggers the fail-closed gate set: compile, static analysis, lint, type check, unit tests, security scan, dependency scan, policy. A skipped required check is a failure.
records.why: Validation is cheap here and expensive in production. Making every gate required is how the platform defines done without a meeting.

records.name: 3. Distributed integration tests
records.what: A coordinator shards suites onto a worker pool and ephemeral environments. Results return to the PR. This is not one CI agent box and not the developer laptop.
records.why: Some truths only appear when services talk to each other. The platform owes you that proof without a shared staging snowflake.

records.name: 4. Build an immutable image
records.what: The build service produces an OCI image from the green SHA. No latest tag. Argo CD will never build this image.
records.why: A digest is the only artifact the rest of the path can agree on. A rebuild per environment is how you lose the ability to say what is running.

records.name: 5. Store the image
records.what: The registry accepts newsfeed-service:v1827 as an immutable digest. If the digest is not here, no pod will start. Promotion is a new pointer, not a rebuild.
records.why: CI writes. The cluster reads. The registry is the contract in the middle.

records.name: 6. Bump deploy manifests
records.what: CI writes the digest into the Deployment in the manifests repo. That write is the deploy. CI still has not talked to Kubernetes.
records.why: Intent that is not in Git is not intent. The bump is how a stored image becomes something Argo CD can see.

records.name: 7. CI ends, CD begins
records.what: CI's job is over: validate, build, store, record. Continuous delivery is the always-on reconciler, not a deploy stage in the same pipeline.
records.why: Keeping CI credentials out of the cluster is a security property and a design property. This badge exists so nobody hides a kubectl behind a job named release.

records.name: 8. Argo CD syncs
records.what: The always-on reconciler diffs the manifests repo against the API server and syncs. Drift from a console click is reversed. This is not a CI job.
records.why: Pull-based delivery is how production stays converged to Git after the humans have gone home.

records.name: 9. Serve user traffic
records.what: The scheduler places pods. Nodes pull the image. A rolling deploy replaces the old replica set. DNS, CDN, load balancer, and ingress shift user traffic onto v1827.
records.why: A digest that never serves a request is a souvenir. This badge is the data-plane proof that the golden path completed.

records.name: Media service
records.what: Images and video metadata. Bytes live in object storage. This service is the index and the authorization gate. News feed and authoring clients call it.
records.why: Putting bytes in pods is how you lose them. Media as a service plus a bucket is the boring design that survives a replica restart. The CDN often fetches the object directly after this service signs the URL.
notes: ×2 typical.
Metadata in its DB. Objects in the bucket.
Talks to object storage and News Feed.
Authorization stays here. The bucket is not public-by-default.

records.name: Notifications service
records.what: Fan-out, push, and email. Domain events on Kafka trigger it. Delivery state and preferences are its store. It talks to external push and email providers and back to User service.
records.why: Synchronous notification on the feed path is how you miss SLOs. An async service lets the feed return and lets retries live where they belong. It is also a blast radius you can page independently.
notes: ×2 typical.
Triggered by the queue, not by the user request that created the post.
Talks to Kafka, User service, and external providers.
Same golden path. Credentials for providers are not in the image.

records.name: Post service
records.what: Create and read posts. News feed and authoring clients call it. Post records live in Cloud SQL. Fan-out hints go on the queue so notifications and indexers do not sit on the write path.
records.why: Posts are the nouns the feed assembles. Owning them in one service keeps the schema and the write path reviewable. The feed should not have a private table of posts.
notes: ×3 typical.
Talks to SQL, Kafka, and News Feed.
Writes are the source of later fan-out.
Same golden path as every other app repo.

records.name: Ranking service
records.what: Rank and candidate generation for the feed. News feed calls it on request paths that need ranking. It stores model features and candidate caches, not the source of posts.
records.why: Ranking is expensive and special, which is why it is not inlined into the feed. Isolating it lets you scale and fail it independently. A ranking outage should degrade, not blank the product.
notes: ×3 typical.
Talks to News Feed, Redis, and feature stores behind the poster.
Cache misses are expected. DB as a ranking backend is not.
Same image-and-GitOps rules. Models are versioned artifacts too.

records.name: User service
records.what: Profile, graph, and authentication. News feed and the edge (session and auth) call it. Identity and graph edges live in Cloud SQL (and a graph store if you have one), not in the pod.
records.why: A feed that cannot name a user is a demo. Isolating identity as its own service keeps authz and graph changes from shipping inside the feed binary.
notes: ×3 typical. Not the traced image, same path.
Talks to SQL, Redis, and News Feed.
Authn at the edge still depends on this service.
Same CI to GitOps contract as news-feed.

records.name: Tempo / Jaeger
records.what: Trace store. A user request that fans out across news-feed, user, ranking, and media is one trace. Sampling decisions are platform policy, applied at the collector.
records.why: Without traces you cannot say where time went, only that it went. Traces are how a staff engineer debugs a golden-path change that compiled, passed tests, and still hurt tail latency.
notes: Vendor-neutral via OTel.
Sampling is a collector concern.
A deploy annotation on a trace is how you prove v1827 caused a shape.
Not a replacement for metrics-based paging.

records.name: Terraform plan and apply
records.what: Terraform creates the infrastructure. Argo CD deploys workloads onto it. Terraform is invoked (plan/apply) and then exits. Cloud resources follow the infra repo. This is a different life cycle from the numbered application path. App developers never run Terraform to ship a feature.
records.why: You need a tool that can mint a VPC and a database. You do not want that tool on the daily path. Making Terraform an explicit, rare, locked operation is how you avoid two writers for the same cloud object and how you keep production credentials off laptops.
notes: plan/apply versus the infra repo, then exit.
Opposite personality from Argo CD (a daemon).
Talks to remote state and to cloud provider APIs.
Not a CI deploy job for application code.

records.name: Remote state, locked
records.what: Remote state (S3 plus DynamoDB lock, or GCS) is the other half of desired infra state. Git is human-readable intent. The backend is what Terraform last believed it created. The lock prevents concurrent apply.
records.why: Without a lock, two applies invent a third reality. Without remote state, laptops become the system of record. This box exists so plane B has a store, just as Git is the store for plane A.
notes: State snapshots and the lock.
Talks to Terraform only.
Not readable as a workflow by product engineers.
A broken lock is an incident, not a retry loop you ignore.

records.name: Internet users
records.what: People opening the product. Their traffic enters through DNS and CDN, then the cloud load balancer, then ingress, then the news-feed API. This is request traffic. It is not a deploy path. A deploy does not start because a user arrived.
records.why: The poster keeps users visible so the data plane has a reason. Control-plane excellence that cannot serve a request is a museum. Users also generate the SLIs that later drive HPA, pages, and the feedback loop.
notes: Users do not trigger CI, Terraform, or Argo CD.
TLS and routing live at the edge, not in the app pods.
This path is drawn on the left so it does not look like a deploy arrow.
Badge 9 sits on this hop: the change is now serving traffic.

records.name: VPC
records.what: The virtual network the cluster and data services share: subnets, routing, security groups, private endpoints. User traffic enters from the edge. East-west traffic between services stays inside. Datastores are not on the public internet.
records.why: Network is policy you can see. A flat, public default is how test data and production credentials leak. Encoding the VPC in Terraform makes the boundary reviewable.
notes: Created by Terraform, not by application CI.
Private nodes, public edge, explicit peering.
Security groups are desired state, not a ticket.
The cluster and the data services live here together.

records.name: Ephemeral workers ×1000s
records.what: Workers are ephemeral slots. A slot exists for the life of one suite, talks to a per-job environment (namespace, compose stack, or preview cluster), and then disappears. The pool implies hundreds to thousands concurrent. Integration tests do not run on the developer laptop and they do not run on a single CI agent.
records.why: Shared staging is where flakes and political blocks are born. Ephemeral per-job environments keep suites isolated and disposable. Scale-out is a worker-pool problem, not a calendar problem.
notes: Nothing durable lives on a worker.
Created for the suite, torn down after the run.
The grid on the poster is the point: this is a fleet, not a box.
Results go back to the PR, not into a tribal spreadsheet.

records.name: Policy / admission — OPA · Kyverno · PSS
records.what: Provenance, registry allow-list, resource limits. Evaluated at CI and again at admit so a bypassed pipeline still cannot land a bad pod.
records.why: Every object create / update against the API server, and the CI policy check.
notes: Policy-as-code (in Git) and admission decisions.
CI (shift-left) and the Kubernetes admission chain.

records.name: Continuously running control plane
records.what: These stay up: Argo CD application controller + repo server; Kubernetes API / scheduler / controllers; OTel collector; policy webhook. Terraform is the opposite — invoked (plan/apply), then exits; its desired infra state still lives in Git + remote state.
records.why: Process supervisors and the cluster itself. Not a cron that “deploys.”
notes: Live control state. Desired state remains in Git.
Each other, the API server, and (for Terraform) the cloud APIs when a human invokes a run.

records.name: API Server
records.what: Desired / actual gateway. Step 10: Kubernetes API accepts the desired Deployment / Service / HPA / Ingress. Every other control loop is a client of this server.
records.why: Argo CD, HPA, Cluster Autoscaler, controllers — not product-engineer laptops in production.
notes: Nothing itself — etcd is behind it.
etcd, admission webhooks, every controller and kubelet.

records.name: News Feed — production application
records.what: A simplified but honest distributed news feed: News Feed, User, Post, Recommendation, Media, and Notification services, plus PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka / Pub/Sub, object storage, and search. Replica ticks sit on the hot path.
records.why: Internet users, via DNS / CDN → cloud LB → ingress / API gateway → News Feed API.
notes: Posts, graphs, media metadata, notification fanout — in the managed data services, not in the pods.
The data services on the right, and OTel on the way out.

records.name: app-newsfeed
records.what: Application code and service config for the news-feed service — the change this diagram traces as PR #4821 and image newsfeed-service:v1827.
records.why: Product engineers.
notes: Source, unit tests, service-level config. Not Kubernetes manifests.
CI on every PR. A green build produces an image; a follow-up write lands in platform-gitops.

records.name: app-users
records.what: Application code and service config for the user / graph / authn service. Same contract as app-newsfeed: code here, manifests in platform-gitops.
records.why: Product engineers.
notes: Source and service config.
CI, then (on green) platform-gitops.

records.name: Watch · compare · sync
records.what: Watch Git (platform-gitops) → compare desired vs actual → sync the cluster (apply / prune / drift). That is the whole job, forever.
records.why: The reconciler’s own loop.
notes: Cache of last-seen Git and live objects.
Git and the Kubernetes API.

records.name: Argo CD
records.what: Always-on reconciler. Watches platform-gitops, diffs desired vs actual, syncs on drift. It is not a CI job and is not “run” per PR. CI updates Git; Argo CD updates the cluster. If someone clicks in the cloud console, drift is detected and the cluster is reconciled back to Git.
records.why: Git changes in platform-gitops, plus its own resync loop. Not the developer, not the CI “deploy” stage.
notes: Application / project cache and sync status. Desired state remains in Git.
Git (watch) and the Kubernetes API server (apply / prune). Never the registry as a builder — it does not build images.

records.name: Arrow of record
records.what: Git (manifests) → Argo CD → Kubernetes API. App deploy is not infra create — see plane B. Product engineers own the numbered path 1–8; platform engineers own plane B.
records.why: A merged gitops change.
notes: The three hops of the arrow are the system of record for workload intent.
Kubernetes API. That is the only write path into the cluster for applications.

records.name: Autoscaling feedback loop
records.what: Traffic up → CPU / RPS up → HPA adds pod replicas. If nodes are packed → Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes. Traffic down → HPA removes pods → CA drains nodes. Signals come from the observability plane, not from CI. HPA and CA run continuously in-cluster.
records.why: SLIs: RPS, latency, error rate, saturation, custom metrics.
notes: Replica and node counts, as live API objects.
Observability backends, API server, cloud provider (for nodes).

records.name: Build Service
records.what: Produces immutable OCI images from a green CI SHA. There is no latest tag in production. The build is a function of the commit; it is not a snowflake run on an engineer’s laptop.
records.why: A green validation graph on the PR / main SHA.
notes: Build cache and provenance for the SHA. The image itself is stored in the registry.
The artifact registry (push). Argo CD never builds images.

records.name: CI platform
records.what: CI is build plus validation. It is triggered by Git push / pull request; there is no manual “run deploy.” On green it publishes an immutable image and then updates the deployment manifest in platform-gitops. It does not mutate production Kubernetes.
records.why: Git. Fail-closed: a red check blocks merge.
notes: Logs, test artifacts, and the pipeline definition (from ci-pipelines). Not images — those go to the registry.
Git (status checks), the distributed test system, the Build Service, the artifact registry, and platform-gitops (step 8).

records.name: CI responsibilities (and non-responsibilities)
records.what: CI compiles, validates, tests, and produces the image. CI does not mutate production Kubernetes. On green: publish an immutable image, then update the deployment manifest in platform-gitops (step 8). Merge of the app PR and the gitops PR are policy-gated.
records.why: Git.
notes: Pipeline logs and the pointer it writes into Git.
Registry (push image) and platform-gitops (write digest). Never the Kubernetes API.

records.name: Validation gates (every PR)
records.what: Compile / build, static analysis, lint, type check, unit tests, SAST, SCA, policy checks. Every PR, no exceptions, fail-closed. A yellow or skipped required check is a failed check.
records.why: The pull request.
notes: Check statuses and retained debug artifacts.
The Git status API. Required statuses block merge.

records.name: ci-pipelines
records.what: CI configuration and reusable pipelines. The fail-closed gate set is defined here once and consumed by every app repo.
records.why: Pipeline authors on the platform team; referenced automatically on every app PR.
notes: Workflow definitions, reusable jobs, policy-as-code hooks.
The CI platform, which loads these pipelines when a Git push or PR arrives.

records.name: Results reported back to the PR
records.what: Status checks plus comments. Required statuses block merge. Artifacts are retained for debug. The PR is the inbox; chat is not the system of record.
records.why: Suite completion.
notes: Status, logs, and debug artifacts.
Git branch protection.

records.name: Cloud provider APIs
records.what: AWS / GCP / Azure APIs. Terraform is the client. This is where a VPC or a database actually comes into existence.
records.why: Terraform apply.
notes: The cloud’s own resource graph (the real world).
The data-plane substrate on the right of this band.

records.name: Cluster Autoscaler
records.what: Node loop. If nodes are packed, CA adds nodes. If traffic falls and HPA removes pods, CA drains idle nodes. Same telemetry plane as HPA.
records.why: Unschedulable pods and underused nodes.
notes: Nothing in-cluster beyond the node objects it requests.
API server and the cloud provider APIs that actually mint VMs. That is the rare moment control plane touches plane B without a Terraform run.

records.name: Kubernetes + network + data services, ready for Argo CD
records.what: VPC, subnets, cluster, nodes, load balancers, databases, object storage, IAM, DNS, secrets, queues — the thing Argo CD deploys onto. Pods, load balancers, databases are data plane. API server, HPA, CA, Argo CD are control plane.
records.why: A successful Terraform apply.
notes: The running cloud account.
Argo CD (once the API server is up) and the application data plane.

records.name: Controller Manager
records.what: The built-in reconcilers: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Service, Job, and the rest. They are why “apply a Deployment” becomes running pods.
records.why: Changes to watched API objects.
notes: Nothing durable outside the API.
API server only.

records.name: Developer environment
records.what: Product engineers write service code on a standardized laptop: language SDK, formatter, linter, typechecker, unit-test runner, platform CLI, golden service templates, local kind/k3d, and secret stubs. Dev tools are a control-plane client, not a tunnel into the cluster.
records.why: The engineer. A commit and an opened pull request are the only human actions on the delivery path. The same CI checks are runnable locally so a push is not the first time a gate is evaluated.
notes: Uncommitted work and feature branches live on the laptop until push. Local kind / k3d clusters are ephemeral and are not a path to production.
Git — commit, push, open PR. Auth is SSO plus short-lived credentials. Developers do not helm-apply or click the cloud console to ship a feature.

records.name: Dev A — software developer
records.what: One of three product engineers on the path. Writes application code, runs the local toolchain, and pushes a branch. The diagram starts with people, not pipelines.
records.why: Own editor, local checks, then git push.
notes: Working tree on the laptop.
Git repositories (app-*).

records.name: Dev B — software developer
records.what: Same role as Dev A / Dev C. The platform does not care which human authored the change; the PR and its required checks are the contract.
records.why: Commit / push.
notes: Local working tree.
Git.

records.name: Dev C — software developer
records.what: Same role as Dev A / Dev B. Multiple authors exist; one change is still traced 1 → 12.
records.why: Commit / push.
notes: Local working tree.
Git.

records.name: Internet path (data plane)
records.what: Users → DNS / CDN → cloud load balancer → ingress / API gateway → News Feed API. This is request traffic, not a deploy path.
records.why: People opening the product.
notes: TLS certs and routing rules (ingress), not application state.
News Feed API, then the six app services.

records.name: Ephemeral test environments
records.what: Per-job namespace, compose stack, or preview cluster. Created for the suite, torn down after the run. This is how integration tests stay isolated without a shared staging snowflake.
records.why: A worker claiming a job.
notes: Short-lived fixtures and seeded data. Gone when the job ends.
The service under test and its fakes / local-data stand-ins.

records.name: Feedback to engineering
records.what: Production telemetry → OTel → Datadog / Prometheus → alerts / SLOs → engineers / platform team. The same path feeds incident response, deployment health, canary analysis, autoscaling signals, capacity planning, SLO error budgets, cost / cardinality, and release rollback.
records.why: Burn-rate, canary shift, infra error (image-pull, admission denial, API latency).
notes: Alert state and SLO error-budget counters.
The people who can merge a gitops rollback or open an infra-terraform change. They do not log into nodes.

records.name: Git — source of truth
records.what: Five repositories hold every desired state the platform converges to. Clusters follow Git; Git does not follow the cluster. A gitops manifest change is how a green image becomes a production intent.
records.why: Developers push application repos and open PRs. CI writes the image digest into platform-gitops on a green build. Platform engineers change infra-terraform.
notes: Application code, service config, deployment manifests, infrastructure definitions, and reusable CI pipelines.
CI (push / PR events), Argo CD (watch platform-gitops), Terraform (read infra-terraform).

records.name: Git repositories (source of truth)
records.what: The five-repo layout is deliberate. Application code does not live next to cluster YAML, and infrastructure does not live next to CI config. Each repo has its own reviewers and merge policy.
records.why: Pushes and pull requests.
notes: The entire desired-state surface of the platform.
CI, Argo CD, Terraform.

records.name: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
records.what: Pod replica loop. Traffic up → CPU / RPS up → HPA adds replicas. Signals come from the observability plane, not from CI. Scale-out is not a Terraform apply and not a CI job.
records.why: Metrics from Prometheus / custom metrics APIs, continuously.
notes: HPA objects and the replica counts it writes onto Deployments.
Metrics APIs and the API server.

records.name: newsfeed-service:v1827
records.what: The concrete artifact this map traces. Digest sha256:9f3a…c21, linux/amd64, 184 MB, immutable. Promotion is a new pointer (build-sha-a1b2 → v1827), not a rebuild. No rebuild between environments.
records.why: A green CI SHA published by the Build Service.
notes: The bytes of the image plus its attestations.
platform-gitops (the digest is written there) and worker nodes (they pull it).

records.name: Second flow — infrastructure
records.what: Platform Engineer → Terraform → remote state → Cloud Provider APIs → network / Kubernetes / LB / DB / storage → cluster ready for Argo CD. If node capacity, a new cluster, or a database must be created, that is this flow. Caption on the diagram: Terraform creates the infrastructure. Argo CD deploys workloads onto it.
records.why: Platform engineers.
notes: infra-terraform + remote state.
The cloud, then (indirectly) Argo CD, which finds an API server that already exists.

records.name: infra-terraform
records.what: Infrastructure definitions as code. This is desired infra state, not desired workload state. App developers never run Terraform to ship a feature.
records.why: Platform engineers, on a deliberate infra change (new node group, new database, new cluster).
notes: VPC, subnets, cluster, node groups, load balancers, databases, IAM, DNS, queues, observability agents — as code.
Terraform plan/apply, which talks to the remote state backend and the cloud APIs.

records.name: Job queue
records.what: Holds the sharded work: newsfeed-it, users-it, contract, e2e-feed, policy-it. Workers pull; the coordinator does not reach into a laptop.
records.why: The scheduler.
notes: Queued and in-flight job records.
Parallel test workers.

records.name: Kubernetes cluster (managed)
records.what: Schedule, restart, scale, service discovery, networking, rolling deploys. The API server is the desired/actual gateway. Controllers converge. This cluster was provisioned by Terraform; Argo CD deploys workloads onto it.
records.why: Argo CD writes desired workload objects. HPA and Cluster Autoscaler write scale decisions from observability signals.
notes: etcd, via the API server: every Deployment, Pod, Service, HPA, Ingress.
kubelets on worker nodes, the cloud provider (via CCM / CA), and Argo CD.

records.name: Kafka / Pub/Sub
records.what: Async fanout — notifications, feed invalidation, downstream indexers.
records.why: Producers in the app services.
notes: Retained streams, not user-facing reads.
Notification, search indexers, any consumer the platform team added.

records.name: Local app code
records.what: The inner loop: newsfeed-service on feature/feed-ranking, a mix of uncommitted edits and a pushed branch. Local work stays on the laptop until push.
records.why: The developer saving and committing.
notes: The working tree and the local branch.
The standardized toolchain (formatter, typechecker, unit tests) and then Git.

records.name: Media Service
records.what: Images / video metadata. Bytes live in object storage; this service is the index and the authorization gate.
records.why: News Feed and authoring clients.
notes: Metadata in its DB; objects in the bucket.
Object storage, News Feed.

records.name: News Feed Service
records.what: Stateless feed assembly. Four replicas on the hot path, HPA-managed. This is the service whose image (v1827) the rest of the diagram traces.
records.why: Ingress / API gateway.
notes: Nothing durable. Reads users, posts, rankings, media metadata.
User, Post, Recommendation, Media, Notification; Redis; the edge.

records.name: Notification Service
records.what: Fanout, push, email.
records.why: Domain events on Kafka / Pub/Sub.
notes: Delivery state and preferences.
The queue, external push / email providers, User Service.

records.name: Object storage
records.what: Media bytes. The Media Service holds metadata and authorization; the bucket holds the objects.
records.why: Media Service and the CDN.
notes: Blobs.
Media Service, CDN / signed URLs.

records.name: Observability platform
records.what: Every production service and Kubernetes node emits metrics, logs, and traces. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral collection layer; backends are interchangeable stores / UX. Do not emit three competing agent stacks per pod. Observability is not a dead end — it feeds engineering.
records.why: The process and the node, continuously. Not a CI step.
notes: Backends: Prometheus (metrics), Grafana (dashboards), Datadog (unified APM), Tempo / Jaeger (traces), Loki / Elasticsearch (logs).
HPA, canary analysis, paging, capacity planning, and the people who shipped 1–12.

records.name: Telemetry backends
records.what: Backends are query/store systems. SLIs (RPS, latency, error rate, saturation) are derived here and drive HPA, canary analysis, and paging — not a dashboard graveyard. Also in: Kubernetes infra metrics (API server, kubelet, node, network) on the same platform.
records.why: The collector, continuously.
notes: Metrics, logs, traces, and the derived SLIs / SLOs.
Alerting, HPA (custom metrics), engineers.

records.name: Collection path
records.what: Apps / K8s nodes → OTel SDK / agent (in-process + node daemon) → OTel collector (always-on control-plane hop) → backends. Agents run on every node (data-plane adjacency, control purpose).
records.why: Emit metrics / logs / traces from every pod and node.
notes: The collector is a fan-out, not a warehouse. Warehouses are the backends.
Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog, Tempo / Jaeger, Loki / Elasticsearch.

records.name: How to read this map
records.what: This is the staff-review architecture of the internal developer platform. Follow the navy badges 1–12 left to right (commit → validate → build → reconcile → run), then down into observability. The colorful canvas is the source of truth; this drawer is the prose layer on top of it.
records.why: A product engineer commits and opens a pull request. That is the only human trigger on the daily delivery path. Nobody runs a deploy job and nobody applies manifests to production from a laptop.
notes: Desired application state lives in Git. Desired infrastructure lives in infra-terraform plus a remote state backend. Immutable images live in the artifact registry. Runtime state lives in the Kubernetes API.

Solid navy arrows are software delivery. Dashed teal is a different life cycle — platform engineers provisioning the cloud. Dotted rose is the learning loop: production talking back to the people who shipped 1–12.

records.name: Platform engineer
records.what: Authors infrastructure as code. Owns plane B. Does not merge application features and does not click-apply production workloads.
records.why: A ticket or a capacity signal that actually requires new substrate.
notes: The infra-terraform working tree.
Terraform.

records.name: platform-gitops
records.what: Deployment manifests — the desired Kubernetes state. Step 8 lands here: CI writes the image digest (newsfeed-service:v1827) into a Deployment. Argo CD is the only process that applies that intent to the cluster.
records.why: CI, after a green image publish. Humans review the gitops PR; they do not apply it.
notes: Deployments, Services, HPA, Ingress, and related desired-state YAML. Not application source.
Argo CD watches this repo continuously.

records.name: Post Service
records.what: Create / read posts.
records.why: News Feed and authoring clients.
notes: Post records in PostgreSQL; fanout hints on the queue.
PostgreSQL, Kafka / Pub/Sub, News Feed.

records.name: PostgreSQL / Cloud SQL
records.what: System of record for users, posts, and the relational slice of the feed. Provisioned by Terraform, consumed by services, never migrated by a CI “deploy” job.
records.why: Application services.
notes: Relational product data.
The services that own the tables. Backups and replicas are plane-B concerns.

records.name: PR #4821 — newsfeed-service
records.what: A first-class object on the path, not a courtesy. Required checks: CI, lint, types, unit, SAST/SCA, policy, integration, review. Merge of the app PR and the later gitops PR are both policy-gated.
records.why: The developer opening the pull request against main. That event starts validation; nothing is deployed yet.
notes: The diff, the review thread, and the check statuses that block merge.
CI (triggered by the PR), the distributed test system (reports back here), and branch protection.

records.name: Promotion (immutable)
records.what: build-sha-a1b2 is retagged to v1827 and referenced from gitops. Nodes pull that digest in step 11. There is no rebuild between environments and no mutable latest.
records.why: A promotion policy, usually on merge to the release branch / main.
notes: Tag → digest mappings.
platform-gitops (the reference that Argo CD will reconcile).

records.name: Recommendation Service
records.what: Rank and candidate generation for the feed.
records.why: News Feed, on each request path that needs ranking.
notes: Model features and candidate caches, not the source of posts.
News Feed, Redis, feature stores behind the diagram.

records.name: Redis
records.what: Cache and short-lived coordination for the feed path.
records.why: Application services.
notes: Ephemeral keys. Not the source of truth.
News Feed, Recommendation, User.

records.name: Central container registry
records.what: Harbor / ECR / GCR / Artifact Registry — treat it as a storage system, not a CI plugin. It sits between CI and the deployment platform. Nodes pull; CI writes. If the digest is not here, Argo CD cannot sync a pod that will start.
records.why: The Build Service pushing a tagged, signed image.
notes: OCI images (app + sidecars), SBOM + provenance attestations, Helm/OCI chart packages, signed tags, retention / promotion policy.
CI (write), worker-node kubelets (pull, step 11), admission policy (registry allow-list).

records.name: What the registry stores
records.what: OCI images (app + sidecars), SBOM + provenance attestations, Helm/OCI chart packages, signed tags, retention and promotion policy. Pull credentials are node identity — not a long-lived secret in a pipeline.
records.why: CI writes; promotion policy moves tags.
notes: The list above. This is the contract the cluster reads.
Admission (allow-list) and kubelet image pull.

records.name: Why the registry sits here
records.what: CI writes. The cluster reads. The registry is the contract: if the digest is not here, Argo CD cannot sync a pod that will start. Image pull is an explicit data-plane hop using the node’s cloud identity.
records.why: Publish from CI; pull from kubelet.
notes: The digest that both sides agree on.
CI, Argo CD (indirectly, via a pod that will fail to start otherwise), worker nodes.

records.name: Remote state backend
records.what: S3 + DynamoDB lock, or GCS. The lock prevents concurrent apply. This is the other half of desired infra state — Git is human-readable intent; the backend is what Terraform last believed it created.
records.why: Every Terraform run.
notes: State snapshots and the lock.
Terraform only.

records.name: Scheduler
records.what: Binds pods to nodes. Step 11 starts here: the scheduler places the new replicaset, then kubelet pulls newsfeed-service:v1827 from the artifact registry.
records.why: Unbound pods in the API.
notes: Bindings, as API objects.
API server. It does not pull images.

records.name: Search
records.what: Index of posts and people. Fed asynchronously from the queue, not from the request path that renders a feed.
records.why: Indexers consuming Kafka / Pub/Sub.
notes: Search documents.
Query path from News Feed / a dedicated search API.

records.name: 1 — Commit from a standardized laptop
records.what: A developer writes newsfeed-service on the platform toolchain and commits. Local checks already match CI. This is the only human trigger that will follow.
records.why: The developer.
notes: The working tree, then the pushed branch.
Git.

records.name: 10 — Kubernetes API accepts desired state
records.what: Deployment, Service, HPA, Ingress are written. Admission (OPA / Kyverno / PSS) evaluates provenance and the registry allow-list again.
records.why: Argo CD apply.
notes: etcd, via the API server.
Scheduler, controllers, admission webhooks.

records.what: Scheduler binds pods. kubelet pulls newsfeed-service:v1827 from the registry using the node’s cloud identity. A rolling deploy replaces the old replicaset; service discovery and the load balancer shift traffic.
records.why: Unbound pods, then kubelet.
notes: Image cache and running containers.
Registry (pull) and the data-plane network (users, databases).

records.what: Each pod and node emits through the OpenTelemetry agent / daemon to the collector and then to backends. SLIs drive HPA, canary, and pages. A bad deploy is rolled back through gitops, not by re-running a deploy script.
records.why: The process, always on.
notes: Backends and SLO counters.
Engineers, HPA, Cluster Autoscaler, and — rarely — Terraform, when capacity is the answer.

records.name: 2 — Desired state in Git
records.what: The change lands in the right repo. Application code goes to app-newsfeed. The five-repo split (app-*, platform-gitops, infra-terraform, ci-pipelines) is the source of truth the rest of the path reads.
records.why: git push.
notes: The commit.
CI, via webhook.

records.name: 3 — PR #4821 becomes the contract
records.what: The pull request is a first-class gate. Required checks (CI, lint, types, unit, SAST/SCA, policy, integration, review) must go green. Nothing has been deployed.
records.why: Opening the PR against main.
notes: The diff and the status checks.
CI and reviewers.

records.name: 4 — Fail-closed validation
records.what: Compile, static analysis, lint, type check, unit tests, SAST, SCA, policy. Fail-closed. A skipped required check is a failure.
records.why: The PR.
notes: Check statuses and artifacts.
Branch protection.

records.name: 5 — Distributed integration tests
records.what: A scheduler shards suites onto a worker pool and ephemeral environments. Results return to the PR. This is not one CI agent box and not the developer laptop.
records.why: CI, as a required gate.
notes: Job state and logs.
The status-check API.

records.name: 6 — Build an immutable image
records.what: The Build Service produces an OCI image from the green SHA. No latest tag. Argo CD will never build this image.
records.why: Green validation.
notes: Build provenance. Bytes go to the registry.
Artifact registry.

records.name: 7 — Store newsfeed-service:v1827
records.what: The registry accepts the immutable digest. Promotion is a new pointer, not a rebuild. If the digest is not here, no pod will start.
records.why: The Build Service push.
notes: Image, SBOM, signatures.
Later: kubelet, on step 11.

records.why: Green image publish.
notes: The manifest in platform-gitops.
Argo CD, which is already watching.

records.name: 9 — Argo CD reconciles
records.what: The always-on reconciler diffs platform-gitops against the API server and syncs. Drift from a console click is reversed. This is not a CI job.
records.why: The gitops commit, plus the resync loop.
