Kubernetes API.

records.name: What is stored where (in Git)
records.what: Application code → app-* repos. Service / app config → app-* plus gitops. Deployment manifests → platform-gitops. Infrastructure definitions → infra-terraform. CI configuration → ci-pipelines. Desired state lives in Git. Clusters converge to Git — not the other way around.
records.why: Authors of each repo, under that repo’s review policy.
notes: The five-repo split above. Do not collapse it.
CI, Argo CD, Terraform — each reads the repo it is allowed to read.

records.name: How telemetry changes engineering behavior
records.what: A bad deploy is a burn-rate alert and a canary metric shift — Argo CD / gitops rollback is the remediation, not a CI re-run of a deploy script. HPA and Cluster Autoscaler consume metrics from this plane. Platform team uses the same telemetry for control-plane health (Argo CD sync, API server latency, image-pull errors, admission denials). Product engineers get paged on their SLOs. Capacity planning (new node groups, bigger DBs) feeds back into plane B: Terraform. That is the rare, deliberate infra change — not the daily feature path.
records.why: SLOs and pages.
notes: The organization’s memory of what shipped and what broke.
Git (rollback PR), Terraform (capacity), and humans.

records.name: Infrastructure provisioning — plane B
records.what: Terraform creates the infrastructure. Argo CD deploys workloads onto it. Distinct from the numbered app-delivery path. App developers never run Terraform to ship a feature. Terraform is invoked (plan/apply) and then exits; Argo CD is a long-running reconciler.
records.why: A platform engineer, when node capacity, a new cluster, or a database must be created. Not a CI “deploy” job.
notes: Desired infra in infra-terraform; last-applied in the remote state backend.
Remote state (lock + state) and the cloud provider APIs, which mint VPC, subnets, cluster, nodes, load balancers, databases, object storage, IAM, DNS, secrets, queues.

records.name: Test scheduler / coordinator
records.what: Shards suites, assigns workers, enforces timeouts and retries. Test orchestration is itself a distributed control plane.
records.why: CI on the PR.
notes: Schedule and lease state for in-flight suites.
The job queue and the worker pool.

records.name: Parallel test workers
records.what: Ephemeral slots (Worker 1…N). The pool implies hundreds to thousands concurrent — integration tests run in parallel workers, not on the developer laptop and not on a single CI agent.
records.why: The job queue.
notes: Nothing durable. A slot exists for the life of one suite.
An ephemeral test environment, then the result sink that comments on the PR.

records.name: Distributed integration test system
records.what: Not a single machine and not “the CI agent box.” A scheduler shards suites, assigns workers, and enforces timeouts and retries. Suites in flight here include newsfeed-it, users-it, contract, e2e-feed, and policy-it.
records.why: CI, as a required gate on the PR.
notes: Job queue state, per-job logs, and a result that is posted back to the PR.
Ephemeral test environments (per-job namespace / compose stack / preview cluster, torn down after the run) and the Git status API.

records.name: Terraform (IaC)
records.what: plan/apply versus infra-terraform. Cloud resources follow Git. Opposite personality from Argo CD: a CLI run, not a daemon.
records.why: Platform engineer (or a tightly gated infra pipeline — still not the app CI).
notes: Nothing itself. State is remote.
Remote state backend and cloud provider APIs.

records.name: Standardized platform toolchain
records.what: Language SDK / runtime, formatter + linter, typechecker, unit-test runner, platform CLI, golden service template, local kind/k3d, secret stubs / SSO. The CLI scaffolds new services from goldens so every repo looks like every other repo.
records.why: The developer, on every save and before every push.
notes: Nothing durable — it is a client, not a system of record.
Local kind/k3d for a cheap inner loop; Git when the change is ready.

records.name: User Service
records.what: Profile, graph, authn.
records.why: News Feed and the edge (session / auth).
notes: Identity and graph edges in PostgreSQL / the graph store.
PostgreSQL, Redis, News Feed.

records.name: Who triggers what
records.what: The engineer commits and opens the PR — that is the only human trigger on the delivery path. CI, tests, and the image build are automated. Argo CD is not invoked by the developer; it watches Git and reconciles continuously.
records.why: Human: PR. Machine: everything after.
notes: Nothing here; this panel is the operating rule.
Git, CI, Argo CD (watch, not invoke). Never the cluster from a laptop.

records.name: Worker nodes — data plane
records.what: Three nodes shown, each with kube-proxy, an OTel agent, and application pods. kubelet pulls newsfeed-service:v1827 from the artifact registry. A rolling deploy replaces the old replicaset; service discovery and the load balancer shift traffic.
records.why: Scheduler bindings and kubelet’s own sync loop.
notes: Container filesystem, image cache, pod network state. Not desired state.
API server (status), artifact registry (image pull), and the node network path to users and datastores.

records.name: How a workload reaches a running prod pod
records.what: 1–8 happen off-cluster (developer → Git → CI → image → gitops manifest). 9 Argo CD reads platform-gitops and diffs against the API server. 10 API accepts the desired Deployment / Service / HPA / Ingress. 11 Scheduler places pods; kubelet pulls newsfeed-service:v1827; rolling deploy replaces the old replicaset; the load balancer shifts traffic. 12 Each pod and node emits metrics, logs, and traces through the OpenTelemetry agent.
records.why: The merged gitops change, then the reconcilers.
notes: Git (intent), registry (bytes), API server (live), backends (telemetry).
Every plane on this map. Continuously running in this boundary: API server, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet, Argo CD, OTel agents, HPA, Cluster Autoscaler, and the application pods themselves.

records.name: Aggregation router
records.what: The first IP hop that has seen more than one access node. It folds OLT and BBU backhaul into fewer wavelengths toward the metro core.
records.why: You do not run a full-table core at every CO. Aggregation is how you keep the core small and the access dumb.
notes: PE or leaf, depending on who sold it.
Holds access VRFs and QoS that the radio and PON already marked.
Uplink is DWDM-colored or grey 100/400G.
Failure domain is a slice of the city, not a rack.

records.name: Anycast + TLS
records.what: The same service address is announced from many PoPs. BGP plus RTT plus health steer the user to a nearby EDGE. TLS is done on the box that won.
records.why: Without anycast, every user pins to one building. With it, a PoP can drain by withdrawing a route.
notes: The user does not pick the PoP. The routing system does.
TLS keys live at the edge. Treat that as a real secret blast radius.
A withdraw is a failover. A bad health check is a stampede.
Cache hit ratio is the only reason this hop is cheap.

records.name: Availability zone
records.what: One AZ is one or more data-center buildings with independent power and cooling from its neighbors. It is a failure domain you can name, not a rack.
records.why: This is the unit you spread across. Two replicas in one AZ are one flood plain.
notes: Independent utility feeds and generators, by design.
A building can be an AZ. A campus of buildings can be an AZ.
Control-plane nodes and etcd members belong in separate AZs.
The worker pool for newsfeed-service lives in these buildings.

records.name: Provider private backbone
records.what: Inter-region traffic between the provider's own buildings rides a private optical backbone, not the public internet. Cross-US is still about 60 to 70 ms RTT. Transatlantic is still 65 to 75 ms.
records.why: Private does not mean faster than glass. It means more control over peering, QoS, and who else is on the fiber.
notes: Same 4.9 μs/km floor. Private is not a wormhole.
Cross-US ~60 to 70 ms RTT. Transatlantic ~65 to 75 ms RTT.
This is the path behind 'multi-region active/active' slides.
Encryption in transit is a policy. Latency is physics.

records.name: BBU (baseband unit)
records.what: The baseband unit sits in the hut or a nearby CO. It runs the MAC and PHY schedule, terminates the radio grant, and emits IP packets onto the backhaul. This is where the request becomes a packet on glass.
records.why: Scheduling lives here. The 1 to 10 ms phone-to-tower number is mostly this box, not the speed of radio.
notes: Bytes become light on the far side of the BBU.
vRAN can move this function into a nearby EDGE hall. The physics do not change.
Clock sync (PTP / GPS) is a real dependency.
After this hop, treat the path as fiber.

records.name: BGP (at the hotel)
records.what: The control plane of interconnection. eBGP sessions over cross-connects and over the IX fabric. This is where prefixes, MED, and communities decide which way the request leaves the building.
records.why: A bad announcement in this hall is a continental event. The data plane is innocent.
notes: Sessions are per-neighbor, over a VLAN or a dedicated jumper.
RPKI and IRR are how you keep a typo from becoming a hijack.
The session is control. The packets still ride the jumper or the IX fabric.
Anycast for the EDGE PoP is a BGP announcement from this same room.

records.name: Carrier cage
records.what: A locked footprint. A carrier or a cloud parks routers, optical gear, and a staff badge policy. Power and cooling are building services. The routers are the tenant's.
records.why: Peering is a conversation between cages, not between logos on a slide. Someone has to rack the box.
notes: Cages are failure domains with keys.
Remote hands can swap a transceiver. They cannot debug your IGP.
Hot and cold aisle still apply. Density is lower than a GPU hall.
The same building may hold a dozen competitors.

records.name: Colo (power, cooling, remote hands)
records.what: The hotel as a landlord: A/B power, chilled water or CRAH, and a remote-hands desk that will reseat a cable at 03:00. Your cage is a tenant. The building is the plant.
records.why: Compute in a hotel is still compute. It dies without power and cooling, and you cannot SSH either of those.
notes: A/B feeds. Know which PDU is which before the truck rolls.
Remote hands are a queue, not an SRE.
Cooling tonnage is the real capacity limit, not floor tile.
The EDGE row next door buys this product.

records.name: Control-plane CPU cell
records.what: A dedicated CPU cell for the Kubernetes API, etcd, and the few boxes that must not drown in tenant noise. Separate failure domain from worker slats. Argo and CI stay ordinary CPU tenants, not guests here.
records.why: etcd on a noisy worker is how you turn a tenant loop into a regional control-plane outage. Put the API somewhere you can name.
notes: CONTROL PLANE badge sits on this cell.
API and etcd are here. Workers are not.
Argo / CI run as ordinary CPU tenants on the data-plane row.
Same rack language. Different blast radius.

records.name: CRAH and hot / cold aisle
records.what: Computer-room air handlers push cold air into a cold aisle. Servers throw heat into a hot aisle. Containment is how you stop the two from mixing.
records.why: Air is a fluid problem. A missing tile is a hot spot. A hot spot is a throttle, then a trip.
notes: CRAH, not 'the AC'. These are precision units on a chilled-water loop.
Hot / cold aisle containment is the design, not a suggestion.
This works for 10 to 15 kW CPU racks. GPU rows outgrow it.
Set points are a capacity knob. Lower is not always better.

records.name: GPU liquid cooling
records.what: Direct-to-chip or rear-door heat exchangers for 40 to 100 kW racks. Air cannot move that heat at a temperature the silicon will accept. CDU (coolant distribution) is now a row-level service.
records.why: Training and inference density is a cooling problem first. If the liquid plant is late, the H100s are sculptures.
notes: 40 to 100 kW per GPU rack, versus 10 to 15 kW typical CPU.
A leak is an incident with a wet floor and a live busway.
CDUs, manifolds, and quick-disconnects are the new PDU.
Ranking (train + infer) lives or dies on this row.

records.name: CPE (ONT / cable modem)
records.what: The customer-premises equipment terminates the last drop. An ONT speaks GPON or XGS-PON. A cable modem speaks DOCSIS. Both hand frames to the access plant toward the central office.
records.why: Without a CPE there is no wireline story. The laptop's Wi-Fi dies at this box. The rest of the poster is photons and colo.
notes: ONT: fiber to the home, then Ethernet to the laptop.
DOCSIS: coax plant, then the same Ethernet handoff.
This box is an ISP asset on the user's power and drywall.
From here the request is serialized onto glass or coax toward the OLT or CMTS.

records.name: CPU slat (worker)
records.what: An ordinary CPU slat in the general row. Same BOM class as its neighbors. The worker node pool is many of these, virtualized.
records.why: You scale the data plane by adding slats and the VMs on them, not by widening a container.
notes: 10 to 15 kW rack budget, air-cooled.
This slat is interchangeable. That is the point.
The panel diagram is the same server to pod stack.
Do not put etcd here.

records.name: Data center (cutaway)
records.what: A building whose job is to keep silicon in spec: power, cooling, and a network that reaches a hotel. Everything the other tabs call a cluster lives on this floor.
records.why: If you cannot draw power and cooling, you do not have a platform. You have a slide.
notes: Power chain on the left of this row. Cooling on the right.
The network fabric and the racks sit on the next rows.
N+1, 2N, and A/B are the words that decide whether a fault is an incident.
Staff should walk one of these before arguing about pod density.

records.name: DWDM (dense wavelength division)
records.what: One fiber pair carries many colors. About 96 or more channels, each a 400G-class wavelength, on a pair. ROADMs switch colors without lighting the packet layer.
records.why: Fiber is scarce. Colors are how you multiply a right of way. Without DWDM, long-haul is a truck roll and a new trench.
notes: ~96+ channels × 400G-class per λ per fiber pair.
A pair is two strands. Capacity is quoted on pairs, not on a single strand.
ROADM sites are huts and hotels, not Kubernetes nodes.
The latency floor is still 4.9 μs/km of glass. Colors do not go faster.

records.name: Tower backhaul
records.what: Fiber (sometimes microwave) from the BBU hut to the metro. After the BBU, the request is light on this lateral.
records.why: A tower without backhaul is a sculpture. This is the hop that puts the cell on the city's ring.
notes: Usually dark fiber or a leased wavelength.
Light in fiber ~204,000 km/s, about 4.9 μs/km one-way.
Microwave is the exception and the backup.
records.medium: Single-mode fiber (or microwave) from the site to metro.
records.latency: 4.9 μs/km one-way of glass, plus the hut.

records.name: Cross-connect jumper
records.what: A yellow jumper in the MMR. Meters of fiber or copper between two cages. Politics measured in weeks. Light measured in nanoseconds.
records.why: This is the hop people call 'peering' when they mean 'a person pulled a cable'.
notes: Meters, not kilometers. Propagation is noise.
Serialization at 100G for 1500 bytes is ~120 ns.
Delivery is remote hands.
records.medium: Single-mode fiber jumper (sometimes copper) in the MMR.
records.speed: ~204,000 km/s over a few meters. Treat as zero.
records.latency: Serialization plus a patch panel. Not 4.9 μs/km in any way that matters.
records.bandwidth: 1/10/100/400G, whatever both cages agreed to light.
records.owner: The hotel sells the jumper. Each tenant owns a side.

records.name: In-rack DAC
records.what: Twinax copper from the server NIC to the ToR. A meter or two. 1 to 5 μs. This is the last electrical hop before most designs go optical again.
records.why: A cheap cable is a real outage class. Label both ends.
notes: In-rack 1–5 μs.
DAC is copper. AOC is light in the same form factor.
Do not drape it through a hinge and then act surprised.
records.medium: Passive twinax DAC (or AOC) inside the rack.
records.speed: Electrical (DAC) over one to three meters.
records.owner: The rack owner. Often the same team as the slat.

records.name: GPON / DOCSIS drop
records.what: CPE to OLT or CMTS. Shared access plant. Serialization at 1G for a 1500-byte packet is about 12 μs. Then propagation is distance.
records.why: Last-mile is a shared medium with a budget. It is not a VPC subnet.
notes: GPON / XGS-PON on fiber, or DOCSIS on coax.
1500-byte packet ~12 μs to serialize at 1G, ~120 ns at 100G.
Then 4.9 μs/km if the drop is glass.
records.medium: PON fiber with splitters, or coax (DOCSIS).
records.speed: ~204,000 km/s on the fiber drop. Coax is slower and shorter.
records.latency: Serialization plus a short plant. Metro has not started.
records.bandwidth: GPON 2.5G down, XGS-PON 10G-class, shared per splitter.

records.name: Inter-AZ hop
records.what: Dark fiber between AZs in the same metro. The budget is under 2 ms RTT. Synchronous replication lives or dies on this number.
records.why: If your 'AZ diversity' path is actually inter-region, you will find out during the first failover.
notes: AZ↔AZ <2 ms RTT.
4.9 μs/km on a metro path.
Provider dark fiber, not the public internet.
records.medium: Provider-owned dark fiber in the metro.
records.bandwidth: Multi-Tb/s campuses. You see a quota, not the pair.

records.name: Inter-region backbone hop
records.what: Provider private backbone between regions. Cross-US ~60 to 70 ms RTT. Transatlantic ~65 to 75 ms RTT. Private is not a wormhole.
records.why: Active/active across regions is a physics statement. The floor is glass.
notes: Cross-US ~60–70 ms RTT.
Transatlantic ~65–75 ms RTT.
NYC↔Chicago ~9 ms one-way if those are the regions.
records.latency: Cross-US ~60–70 ms RTT. Transatlantic ~65–75 ms RTT.
records.bandwidth: ~96+ channels × 400G-class per λ per pair, times many pairs.

records.name: Long-haul terrestrial hop
records.what: Intercity glass in a rail, highway, or pipeline right of way. EDFA every 80 to 100 km. The path is longer than the map.
records.why: NYC to Chicago is ~9 ms one-way because the fiber is ~1,200 km, not because BGP is shy.
notes: NYC↔Chicago ~9 ms one-way (fiber path ~1,200 km).
Cross-US ~60–70 ms RTT.
EDFA every 80–100 km.
records.medium: DWDM on terrestrial fiber in a shared right of way.
records.speed: ~204,000 km/s. Colors do not go faster.
records.latency: 4.9 μs/km one-way. NYC to Chicago ~9 ms. Cross-US ~60–70 ms RTT.
records.bandwidth: ~96+ channels × 400G-class per λ per fiber pair.
records.owner: Long-haul carrier. The RoW is often a railroad or a pipeline.

records.name: Metro ring hop
records.what: Around the city on the ring. Aggregation to metro core. DWDM may already be coloring the pair.
records.why: This is the 1 to 2 ms most 'local' calls actually pay.
notes: Metro ring 1–2 ms.
4.9 μs/km of glass. A 40 km ring is ~200 μs of light.
The rest is routers and protection switch.
records.medium: Metro dark fiber or DWDM, often a ring.
records.bandwidth: 100/400G-class, many colors if DWDM is up.
records.owner: Metro carrier or the access ISP's transport arm.

records.name: NVLink (GPU to GPU)
records.what: Inside the node, GPU to GPU. Hundreds of nanoseconds at about 900 GB/s. This is not Ethernet and it is not a CNI plugin.
records.why: If the train is waiting on AllReduce, this hop and the IB/RoCE hop next to it are the floor.
notes: GPU↔GPU ~100s of ns at ~900 GB/s.
NVLink is inside the tray. IB/RoCE is between trays.
You cannot peer this with a ToR and a hope.
records.medium: NVLink copper/organic inside the GPU complex.
records.speed: ~900 GB/s class, hop latency in hundreds of ns.
records.owner: The GPU node BOM. NVIDIA's interconnect, in this telling.

records.name: PNI (private network interconnect)
records.what: A dedicated interconnect between two networks, usually in this hotel, usually on a cross-connect plus a bilateral BGP session. Not the IX fabric.
records.why: When traffic is large and steady, PNI is cheaper and cleaner than IX ports or transit.
notes: Bilateral, not multilateral.
Same jumper physics as e-crossconnect, plus a session.
Used between clouds, CDNs, and carriers.
records.medium: Dedicated fiber jumper (PNI) in a hotel or a campus.
records.latency: Hotel-local. Serialization at 100G is ~120 ns per frame.
records.bandwidth: 100/400G-class ports, often several in a bundle.
records.owner: The two networks. The hotel bills the cross-connect.

records.name: EDGE PoP to region
records.what: Cache miss. The PoP fetches from origin in the region on provider or carrier glass. This may be metro (1 to 2 ms) or long-haul if the origin is in another city.
records.why: A miss turns an EDGE win into a regional RTT. Hit ratio is the only reason the EDGE row exists.
notes: Metro if origin is in-city: 1–2 ms.
Otherwise the long-haul numbers apply.
TLS may already be done at the PoP.
records.medium: Metro or long-haul fiber from the hotel toward the AZ campus.
records.latency: Metro 1–2 ms, or the long-haul floor if origin is far.
records.bandwidth: 100/400G-class, often a PNI into the cloud.
records.owner: CDN or cloud EDGE team, plus the transport provider.

records.name: RF hop (phone to tower)
records.what: The handset to the RRU. Licensed LTE or 5G NR in air. The bytes are radio. They are not yet light.
records.why: People blame distance. On this hop, RF is essentially c. The number you feel is the scheduler.
notes: RF ≈ c. A city cell is microseconds of air.
HARQ and the grant sit in the 1 to 10 ms.
After the BBU the medium changes.
records.medium: Licensed cellular radio (LTE / 5G NR) in air.
records.speed: ≈ c in air. Not the floor you will feel.
records.latency: 1–10 ms phone to tower (scheduling, not distance).
records.bandwidth: Tens to hundreds of Mbps per user, shared on the sector.
records.owner: Mobile network operator. The handset is the user's.

records.name: Subsea hop
records.what: Wet glass. Repeaters every 60 to 80 km, powered at about 10 kV DC from the landing station. Transatlantic RTT is 65 to 75 ms.
records.why: There is no alternative medium. Satellites are a different poster and a worse number.
notes: Repeaters 60–80 km, shore ~10 kV DC.
Transatlantic ~65–75 ms RTT.
A cut is a ship, not a ticket.
records.speed: ~204,000 km/s in the fiber, in a cable that is not a straight line.
records.latency: Transatlantic ~65–75 ms RTT. Floor is still 4.9 μs/km.
records.bandwidth: DWDM on a handful of pairs. 400G-class per λ.
records.owner: Cable consortium. Landing parties on each shore.

records.name: ToR to spine to ToR
records.what: Inside the building Clos. East-west between racks. ECMP over 100/400G. This is the hop your service mesh cannot optimize away.
records.why: If two pods in the same AZ are slow, look here before you look at Go channels.
notes: ToR→spine→ToR 5–50 μs.
1500-byte packet ~120 ns to serialize at 100G.
ECMP on 5-tuple. One flow, one path.
records.medium: DAC / AOC in-rack, then single-mode or AOC up the Clos.
records.speed: Electrical on DAC, then light on the uplink.
records.latency: 5–50 μs ToR to spine to ToR.
records.owner: The cloud or colo network team.

records.name: Wi-Fi hop (laptop to CPE)
records.what: Unlicensed radio from the laptop to the CPE. Same physics as other RF: ≈ c, and contention dominates.
records.why: The laptop path has to join the glass story at the CPE. This hop is the join.
notes: RF ≈ c. Airtime and retries are the delay.
The CPE is the media converter.
After this, treat the path as wireline.
records.medium: Unlicensed Wi-Fi (802.11) in air, then Ethernet to the CPE.
records.speed: ≈ c in air, then a short copper jumper.
records.latency: Airtime and retries dominate. Distance does not.
records.bandwidth: Shared channel. Hundreds of Mbps typical in a home.
records.owner: The user owns the AP. The ISP owns the CPE behind it.

records.name: EDFA (erbium-doped fiber amplifier)
records.what: Every 80 to 100 km an erbium-doped amplifier boosts the wavelengths without converting them to packets. Huts, power, and a padlock. No IP address you will ever ping.
records.why: Glass eats light. Without EDFAs the long-haul row is a dark line on a slide.
notes: Spacing: 80 to 100 km terrestrial.
Optical, not electrical regeneration, on modern routes.
Each hut is power, HVAC, and a generator or a very long battery.
A failed amplifier is a color outage across a state.

records.name: EDGE cloud / CDN PoP
records.what: A small compute and cache footprint inside the hotel or a nearby hall. TLS terminates here. The cache hopes the object is already on disk. Anycast brought the user to this city.
records.why: This is the first place the request may be answered without crossing a region. If the feed is cacheable, the region never sees the byte.
notes: Sits in the hotel so it can peer richly and terminate close to the user.
Not a full AZ. A handful of racks, a cache, and a tight failure domain.
Misses go to the region on the next hop.
The EDGE badge on the poster is this box.

records.name: DC border
records.what: The building's north-south edge. Provider backbone and peering land here. Southbound is the spine. This is not the ToR, and it is not the IXP. It is the DC's front door.
records.why: If every flow hairpins at one pair of border routers, that pair is your region-sized blast radius.
notes: eBGP toward the backbone and toward other buildings.
Default-free or nearly, depending on the provider.
DDoS and ACL policy belong here, not on every leaf.
The packet is still on glass. The next hop is the Clos.

records.name: Leaf
records.what: The leaf is the other side of the Clos. It faces a row of ToRs or, in some designs, is the ToR. BGP in the DC carries reachability. No STP novel.
records.why: Leaf-spine is the contract. Overlay (VPC, Geneve) sits on it. The underlay has to be boring.
notes: BGP-in-DC is the control plane. The data plane is IP or MPLS.
Oversubscription is a stated number, not a surprise.
A leaf is a row-level failure domain.
Server default gateway is usually an anycast VTEP on this tier.

records.name: Spine (Clos)
records.what: Non-blocking Clos spine. Every leaf can reach every leaf in a bounded number of hops. ECMP sprays flows. There is no 'core VLAN' story left to tell.
records.why: A spine is how you keep east-west cheap inside the building. Without it you invent hairpins and then you invent outages.
notes: ToR to spine to ToR is 5 to 50 μs.
ECMP on 5-tuple. One fat flow is still one path.
Spines do not run your stateful services. They forward.
Failure of one spine is a loss of hash buckets, not a partition, if you built it right.

records.name: GPON / DOCSIS access plant
records.what: The last-mile plant. GPON and XGS-PON share a feeder fiber with splitters. DOCSIS shares a coax tree. Both concentrate many homes onto one OLT or CMTS port at the central office.
records.why: Access is a shared medium with a budget. Contention here is not a pod problem.
notes: XGS-PON is 10G-class. Classic GPON is 2.5G down.
DOCSIS 3.1 and 4.0 push gigabit on coax that already exists.
Splitters are passive. The OLT holds the intelligence.
Serialization at 1G for a 1500-byte packet is about 12 μs. Then propagation is distance.

records.name: GPU slat (H100 class)
records.what: A dense tray: GPUs, NVLink, a CPU complex that exists to feed them, and a NIC that speaks IB or RoCE. The pod that lands here is a train or a heavy infer, not the newsfeed worker.
records.why: Same virtualization story, different thermal and fabric contract. Do not schedule this like a 1U CPU.
notes: NVLink inside. IB or RoCE east-west.
Liquid first. Air is a backup story at this density.
The panel diagram still applies: hypervisor, VM, kubelet, pod.
Ranking train and infer share this slat class.

records.name: Carrier hotel
records.what: A building whose product is interconnection. 60 Hudson in New York, 350 East Cermak in Chicago, One Wilshire in Los Angeles. Meet-me rooms, carrier cages, an IXP, and colo halls under one roof.
records.why: This is where networks meet without digging a street. If your packet changes providers, it often does it in a building like this.
notes: Not a cloud region. A real-estate and cross-connect business.
Tenants bring their own routers. The building sells power, cooling, and copper or fiber jumpers.
A fire or a flood here is a multi-provider event.
The EDGE PoP in the next row often sits in this same hall.

records.name: Hypervisor (KVM)
records.what: KVM on the slat. It carves VMs that the platform treats as Kubernetes nodes. The physical NIC is shared through a virtual switch, or given away through SR-IOV, or offloaded to a DPU.
records.why: Multi-tenancy starts here. If the hypervisor is a pet, the node pool is a lie.
notes: KVM is the default story. The contract is a VM that looks like a node.
vswitch vs SR-IOV is a latency and isolation choice.
A DPU can move vswitch and storage off the host CPUs.
Live migration is a policy, not a right, on GPU slats.

records.name: Inter-AZ dark fiber
records.what: Provider-owned dark fiber between AZs in the same metro. Budget is under 2 ms RTT. This is why a regional database sync is plausible and a cross-region one is not.
records.why: Synchronous replication has a physics budget. Inter-AZ is inside it. Inter-region is not.
notes: AZ to AZ <2 ms RTT.
Dark fiber: the provider lights it. You do not see the wavelengths.
Distance is metro, not long-haul, but the path still is not a straight line.
A metro cut that hits two AZ laterals is the nightmare scenario.

records.name: IXP and route servers
records.what: An Internet exchange: a shared layer-2 fabric and a pair of route servers. Members peer over the fabric. The route server is a convenience, not a requirement. Many still run bilateral BGP.
records.why: Public peering is how you skip transit for a slice of traffic. The IXP is a switch and a policy, sitting in this hotel.
notes: Route servers simplify multilateral peering. They do not forward packets.
The forwarding path is member-to-member on the IX fabric.
Port speed is 100G-class and climbing.
An IX outage is a traffic shift onto transit, not a dark user.

records.name: Cable landing station
records.what: The beach manhole and the building behind it. High-voltage DC plant for the repeaters, power feed equipment, and a backhaul lateral to the nearest carrier hotel or metro core.
records.why: You do not land a cable in a cloud region. You land it in a hardened hut, then you buy glass to a hotel.
notes: PFE (power feed equipment) is the interesting kit.
Beach manhole, then a duct into the station.
From here it is terrestrial again: laterals toward hotels.
Permitting and a beach are the long pole, not the transceiver.

records.name: Long-haul terrestrial
records.what: Intercity glass in a right of way: rail, highway, pipeline. The path is longer than the map. NYC to Chicago is about 1,200 km of fiber for ~9 ms one-way, not the great-circle distance.
records.why: p99 between regions is this path plus the amplifiers on it. You cannot kubectl your way around a railroad.
notes: Right of way follows someone else's trench.
NYC to Chicago ~9 ms one-way on ~1,200 km of fiber.
Cross-US ~60 to 70 ms RTT.
Diverse paths matter. Two wavelengths in one conduit are one backhoe.

records.name: Metro core
records.what: A handful of sites that hold the city's default route toward long-haul and toward the carrier hotels. Full-ish tables. This is where DWDM stops being optional.
records.why: If every packet to another city hairpins through one building, that building is a blast radius with a street address.
notes: Usually two to four buildings, not twelve.
Peers into hotels and into the long-haul ROADM layer.
DWDM starts in earnest on the far side.
Staff should know which two buildings those are.

records.name: Metro fiber ring
records.what: A ring (or a mesh that pretends to be a ring) around the city. Aggregation sites sit on it. One cut should not isolate a CO. Latency around a metro is 1 to 2 ms.
records.why: Metro is where last-mile access becomes a city. If the ring is thin, every later number is a lie.
notes: 1 to 2 ms typical around a metro.
Light in fiber is ~204,000 km/s, about 4.9 μs/km one-way.
A 40 km ring is ~200 μs of glass. The rest is nodes.
Protection switching is why it is a ring and not a spur.

records.name: Meet-me room (MMR)
records.what: The room where the building's interconnects are documented and pulled. Carriers, clouds, and enterprises meet on a panel, not on the public internet.
records.why: Without an MMR you are running patch cords across a loading dock. The MMR is how a hotel stays a hotel.
notes: Every cross-connect is a work order and a monthly bill.
Physical access is badged and escorted. This is not a self-serve VPC console.
The MMR is a blast radius. Treat it like a spine.
Photos of the panel are a security incident.

records.name: newsfeed-service:v1827
records.what: The same artifact Golden path ships. Image digest from the registry, manifest from platform-gitops, applied by Argo, running in this pod on a VM on a CPU slat in an AZ.
records.why: The whole poster exists so this process can answer the thumb. If you cannot follow the request to this box, the other tabs are fiction.
notes: Same image tag the golden path produced.
Stateless worker. Horizontal. CPU row, not GPU.
p99 the user feels is every hop above this, plus this process.
Observe it from the other tabs. Power it from this one.

records.name: OLT / CMTS at the CO
records.what: The optical line terminal (or CMTS) lives in a central office. It terminates thousands of ONTs or modems and hands IP up to the metro aggregation router.
records.why: This is the first telco building that looks like a small data hall: DC power, transmission bays, and a meet-me toward metro fiber.
notes: CO, not a cloud AZ. Different union, different keys, different fire code.
Uplink is usually 100G-class toward the metro ring.
The OLT is the last hop that still knows about PON grants.
From here the packet is just an IP frame on metro glass.

records.name: How to read this map (metal)
records.what: This tab is the metal under the other four. The golden path's worker node is a VM on a slat in a rack in an AZ. Follow navy badges 1 through 13: thumb, tower, wireline, metro, long-haul, subsea, carrier hotel, EDGE, region, power and cooling, fabric, racks, server. p99 has a floor: 4.9 μs per km of glass.
records.why: Logical diagrams hide the floor. A 70 ms US RTT is not a Kubernetes problem. It is glass, amplifiers, and a path that is longer than the map. Staff review starts here when someone asks why the feed feels slow from another continent.
notes: Every hop is a transformation: radio to light to electrons to light.
Graphite boxes are buildings and racks. Blue edges are photons in fiber. Teal is the data plane. Navy is control.
Tap a box or a link. Edge panels carry medium, speed, latency, bandwidth, and owner.
Click a server slat for the VM and pod stack. The pod is newsfeed-service:v1827.

records.name: Pod (namespaces + cgroups)
records.what: A pod is cgroups and namespaces on the node, plus a pause container and one or more app containers. It is not a VM. It is a scheduled slice of a VM that is already a slice of a slat.
records.why: If you think a pod 'is the server', you will overbook the slat and then you will page.
notes: Namespaces isolate the view. cgroups isolate the budget.
The sandbox is only as strong as the runtime and the node.
CNI gives the pod an address on the vswitch (or SR-IOV).
The request that started on a thumb lands here.

records.name: Diesel generators
records.what: On-site generators that hold the building when the utility does not. Fuel, air, and a test schedule. Start time is why the UPS exists.
records.why: A generator that has not been tested under load is a statue. Compliance is a monthly crank, not a PDF.
notes: Fuel logistics are the long outage. 24 to 72 hours on site is common.
N+1 or 2N. A, B, and the leftover.
Emissions and neighbors are real constraints on how long you can run.
ATS (automatic transfer) is the control plane of this hop.

records.name: PDUs, busway, A/B to the rack
records.what: Power distribution units and busway carry A and B feeds down the aisle to each rack. Dual-corded servers sip both. A single-corded box is a choice to fail with one side.
records.why: The last ten meters of power are where most 'mystery' reboots hide. Label the whip.
notes: A/B diversity dies if both cords land on one PDU.
Busway beats a spaghetti of whips in a dense hall.
Typical CPU rack is 10 to 15 kW. GPU rows are 40 to 100 kW.
N+1 and 2N are meaningless if the rack is single-fed.

records.name: UPS
records.what: Uninterruptible power: batteries or a rotary, plus inverters. It rides through the seconds while diesel cranks. It does not ride through an hour.
records.why: The UPS is a bridge, not a generator. Treat battery runtime as a measured number, not a hope.
notes: Seconds to a few minutes, by design.
N+1 or 2N UPS blocks. Know which halls share a block.
A failed inverter is a step load onto the remaining side.
Downstream is the PDU and the busway, not the rack yet.

records.name: Utility, transformers, switchgear
records.what: Medium-voltage utility service, on-site transformers, and switchgear that make the building's AC bus. This is the first box in the power chain. Everything downstream is a customer of this hop.
records.why: A utility sag is a building event. The UPS exists because this hop is not clean.
notes: Two utility feeds if you are lucky and the street allows it.
Transformers are a lead-time item measured in months.
Switchgear is the last place a human can isolate a hall.
This is not software. The runbook is a lockout tag.

records.name: General CPU row (stateless / K8s workers)
records.what: Standard 1U and 2U dual-socket servers. 10 to 15 kW per rack. This is the golden-path worker node pool: VMs on these slats, kubelets on those VMs, pods on those kubelets.
records.why: If you cannot point at a row and say 'stateless compute lives here', the platform is a rumor.
notes: DATA PLANE badge sits on this row.
Air-cooled. Hot / cold aisle is enough.
Argo and CI are tenants on ordinary CPU, not a special hall.
Click a slat for the server to VM to pod stack.

records.name: GPU row (H100, NVLink, IB / RoCE)
records.what: H100-class trays, NVLink inside the node, InfiniBand or RoCE between nodes. 40 to 100 kW per rack. Liquid cooling. This is where ranking trains and where the heavy infer sits.
records.why: A GPU row is a different building product. If you treat it like a CPU row you will trip breakers and then you will miss a train.
notes: 40 to 100 kW versus 10 to 15 kW typical.
NVLink GPU to GPU is hundreds of ns at about 900 GB/s.
The fabric next to the Ethernet Clos is IB or RoCE.
Click a GPU slat for the same server-to-pod story, with a different BOM.

records.name: Memory-optimized row (Postgres, Redis)
records.what: Fewer sockets, much more DRAM, and a NUMA story. Postgres and Redis sit here because a cache miss to disk is an incident and a cache miss to a remote rack is a tax.
records.why: Stateful latency is a memory and a locality problem. You do not put the primary on a noisy GPU row to save a floor tile.
notes: DIMM population and channel count are the capacity plan.
These slats still look like 1U. The BOM is different.
Failure domain is the replica set, not the row, if you placed it that way.
Same ToR and same DAC rules as the CPU row.

records.name: Storage-dense row (object / JBODs)
records.what: JBODs and dense NVMe chassis. Object storage, image layers, and the cold side of the newsfeed. Power is media plus controllers, not GPUs.
records.why: Bytes at rest have a floor too: rebuild time, rack weight, and a busway that can feed a lot of drives.
notes: Weight is a structural limit. These rows are heavy.
Rebuild and rebalance are the real SLO, not raw GB.
Object is the artifact store behind newsfeed-service:v1827.
Do not mix this density with liquid GPU manifolds on the same row.

records.name: TPU pods (GCP variant)
records.what: Google's custom silicon in a dedicated optical mesh. A TPU 'pod' is a machine-room product, not a Kubernetes pod. The interconnect is optical and closed.
records.why: This row exists so the poster tells the truth on GCP. You do not ECMP your way into a TPU slice from a random ToR.
notes: Dedicated optical mesh, not the DC Ethernet Clos.
Scheduler and quota are a different control plane.
Cooling and power look more like the GPU row than the CPU row.
A Kubernetes pod that 'uses a TPU' is a claim on this hall.

records.name: Region (metro of 3+ AZs)
records.what: A cloud region is a metro: three or more availability zones, each one or more data-center buildings, tied by the provider's dark fiber. It is not a single address.
records.why: People say 'us-east-1' as if it were a room. It is a set of buildings and a fiber ring with a product name.
notes: Three AZs is the usual contract for a regional control plane.
Inter-AZ is dark fiber, under 2 ms RTT.
Inter-region rides the provider private backbone, not the public internet, for east-west.
Your VPC drawing sits on this metal.

records.name: RRU (remote radio unit)
records.what: The remote radio unit sits in the wind, on the mast, next to the antennas. It turns baseband samples into RF and back. CPRI or eCPRI carries those samples down to the BBU.
records.why: You put the RF as close to the antenna as you can. Cable loss at radio frequencies is why the RRU is not in the hut.
notes: Mast-mounted. Weather, lightning, and a hoist are the ops model.
eCPRI can ride Ethernet and Ethernet can ride fiber.
The air interface ends here. Below this, it is a transport problem.
A failed RRU is a sector outage, not a Kubernetes event.

records.name: Physical server (slat)
records.what: A 1U or 2U slat: NIC, CPUs, RAM, local NVMe. Dual cords on A/B. DAC to the ToR. This is the machine. Everything above it is software you could lose on a reboot.
records.why: The golden-path worker node is not this slat. It is a VM on this slat. Click through the diagram in the panel.
notes: NIC, two sockets, DRAM, a few NVMe devices.
SmartNIC or DPU can offload vswitch, crypto, and storage.
SR-IOV bypasses the vswitch when the workload paid for it.
newsfeed-service:v1827 will run in a pod on a VM on this box.
